All 100 simulations are used. The best design scores a mean L/D of **116.5**, which is about 25% better than NACA 4412 (93.5). None of the last 92 designs failed; the only failures were two in the third batch.

**Best design:** `u = [0.30, 0.50, 0.57, 0.70, 0.50, 0.64, 0.71]`
- In physical terms: a0 ≈ 0.60, a2 ≈ 0.95, a3 ≈ 1.11; b ≈ [0.18, 0.10, 0.156, 0.184].
- Shape: maximum thickness at 41% chord, maximum camber 3.6% at about 55% chord.

| CL | alpha | cd | L/D | cm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | −0.78° | 0.00519 | 77.1 | −0.121 |
| 0.6 | 1.28° | 0.00495 | 121.2 | −0.116 |
| 0.8 | 2.64° | 0.00529 | 151.2 | −0.128 |

The last few steps were still gaining about 0.5 per step. The true optimum is probably a little further along that direction (lower b2, higher b3), but the budget ran out before I could pin it down.

**What I learned about the design space**

1. **Camber amount is the biggest lever, and it's a trade between the two ends of the CL range.** About 3.5–3.7% camber was best. More camber pushes the CL 0.8 point well into the low-drag range (L/D up to 153). But it puts CL 0.4 at negative alpha, where drag rises on the lower surface, and L/D there drops to about 70. Because CL 0.8 counts most in the mean, the optimum leans toward the high-CL end, and CL 0.4 always stays weak at roughly 72–80.

2. **Where the maximum thickness sits is set by a laminar-flow benefit against a stall cliff.** Moving it from 33% to about 40–43% chord lowered drag at every CL by keeping the flow laminar longer. Beyond about 47%, the low-drag range no longer reached CL 0.8: drag there jumped to about 0.016, or XFoil failed to converge. Those were the only failures in the whole run. A blunt leading edge (high a0) pulled the thickness forward and cost about 20 L/D.

3. **Thickness settings sit on a ridge, not a single peak.** A sharper leading edge (lower a0) combined with less aft thickness (lower a2) keeps the maximum thickness near 40% and scores as well or better. Moving along that ridge gained about 1 point. The trailing-edge wedge a3 has a narrow sweet spot near u ≈ 0.57. Values of 0.7 or more cost a lot (down to 104–108), because the steeper rear recovery adds drag at CL 0.6 and 0.8.

4. **How the camber is spread matters slightly.** Uniform camber weights beat both front-loaded and simple aft-loaded camber. The best pattern was a mild zigzag: b0 and b2 high, b1 lower, and a little extra weight on b3 at the trailing edge. That adds lift without a large pitching moment (cm about −0.12 to −0.13). Taking weight from b2 and giving it to b3 produced the final gains. An extreme zigzag hurt CL 0.4.

5. **The top of the landscape is flat.** Every design from about the 40th simulation onward scored 112–116.5. Big jumps away from it (very thin aft section, blunt leading edge, extreme camber patterns) found no better region.
